Why do some places use photovoltaic cells as solar power and others use solar thermal power instead?

It used to be the convention that solar thermal, or 'solar-dynamic' as they're also called, system were generally more cost-efficient but didn't scale well and couldn't accommodate variable terrain, needing very large very flat locations. So they were favored for the largest installations in the most ideal locations. Being usually steam turbine based, they could more readily produce AC power and more easily integrate to the grid. They also have the advantage that, at a certain size, they can store heat to carry power production through the night and so operate more continuously. This is especially true of solar salt pond systems favored by remote desert industry but not normally used for municipal power because of the environmental hazards. Photovoltaics rely on semiconductor materials needing sophisticated fabrication methods whereas solar-thermal systems are based on more-or-less common steam turbine power systems. (tech going back to the 19th century when solar thermal steam engines were first invented ) They had shorter duty lives compared to the more resilient lower-tech hardware. They also produce power as DC and so, at large scales, need sophisticated large scale power inverter systems that didn't become common until the advent of practical High Voltage DC long distance power transmission. However, photovoltaics had lower maintenance, were less bothered by varying terrain and scaled more freely and so have been preferred for mountain/hill country, homes, individual building, and remote installations.

Today, the up-front costs of producing photovoltaics has dropped greatly while their performance and lifespan has greatly increased and so the choice is not as clear. At large scales they're still more expensive up-front but have a great maintenance cost advantage that can lead to better net cost-efficiency. Solar thermal has also advanced and more recent mirror and tower heliostat array systems (not a new idea, but made more practical recently by computer controlled multi-axis mirror mounts) have eliminated the need for vast plumbing arrays common to the earlier forms of 'trench' collectors while also allowing for active sun tracking for better performance. Self-contained microturbine and Sterling engine based solar thermal generators are also allowing solar thermal tech to reach smaller cost-effective scales, though these still haven't proven suited to household installations and sacrifice the ability to store heat. (very recent introduction of municipal scale power storage or 'energy buffer' systems make this less critical) So the question of choice for these has become much more complicated. Often the choice may depend on topographical details of the regional location, the nature of the regional grid, what kind of large scale discounts a municipality or government project can get between imported and domestic manufacturers, and--of course--politics.
